ety.text: Synchronically equivalent to tight + -en, but actually derived from Middle English tighten, from Old English tyhtan, thus originally unrelated to tight (Old English *þiht).

ex: Please tighten that screw a quarter-turn.
Just where I please, with tighten;d rein / I'll urge thee round the dusty plain.
That joint is tightening as the wood dries.

senses.d: To make money harder to borrow or obtain.
ex: If the government doesn't tighten the money supply, inflation is certain to be harsh.
The Fed is expected to tighten by a quarter-point.

grp.label: to make money harder to obtain

Proto-West Germanic *tīgr Old English tigras Middle English tygre English tiger From Middle English tygre, in part from Old English tigras (pl.), in part from Anglo-Norman tigre, both from Latin tigris, from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris), from Iranian (compare Avestan 𐬙𐬌𐬔𐬭𐬌 (tigri, “arrow”), 𐬙𐬌𐬖𐬭𐬀 (tiγra, “pointed”)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to pierce, prick, be sharp”). Compare English stick.
From the mascot of Princeton (a tiger), which led to early cheerleaders calling out "Tiger" at the end of a cheer for the Princeton team.

senses.d: Panthera tigris, a large predatory mammal of the cat family, indigenous to Asia.
A male tiger; as opposed to a tigress.
ex: Coordinate term: tigress

senses.d: A sabre-toothed tiger (any felid in the subfamily †Machairodontinae).
A tiger moth in the family Arctiidae.
Any of the three Australian species of black-and-yellow striped dragonflies of the genus Ictinogomphus.
A tiger butterfly in the tribe Danaini, especially subtribe Danaina.
A representation of a large mythological cat, used on a coat of arms.
A final shouted phrase, accompanied by a jump or outstretched arms, at the end of a cheer.
ex: . . . every blue coat in the audience sprang to his feet, with three times three and a tiger.

From Middle English tight, tyght, tyȝt, tiht, variants of thight, thiht, from Old English *þiht, *þīht (attested in meteþiht), from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tenkt- (“dense, thick, tight”), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, pull”). Cognate with Scots ticht, West Frisian ticht, Danish tæt, Icelandic þéttur (“dense”), Norwegian tett, Swedish tät, Dutch dicht (“dense”), German dicht (“dense”).
From Middle English tighten, thyhten (“to make tight”); see tighten.

senses.d: Firmly held together; compact; not loose or open.
ex: a tight sponge; a tight knot
Pull your seatbelts tight before takeoff.
tight control on a situation
Make sure to pull the rope tight.
I grew up in a poor neighborhood; money was very tight, but we made do.
We've grown tighter over the years.
The drawbacks of being in a too-tight couple (there's no room to blow your nose)
He's a bit tight with his money.
You say he's a Jew, does it mean that he's tight?

senses.d: Narrow, such that it is difficult for something or someone to pass through it.
ex: The passageway was so tight we could barely get through.
They flew in a tight formation.

senses.d: Fitting close, or too close, to the body.
ex: tight clothing;  a tight coat;  My socks are too tight.

senses.d: Of a turn, sharp, so that the timeframe for making it is narrow and following it is difficult.
ex: The mountain pass was made dangerous by its many tight corners.

senses.d: Firmly, so as not to come loose easily.
ex: Hold on tight to the rope.
'I had my eyes tight shut.'
Good night, sleep tight.

grp.label: under high tension — see also taut
fitting close, or too close, to the body — see also tight-fitting
